angle: The delay-of-gratification studies are usually told as a story about willpower, but Kidd, Palmeri & Aslin (2013) showed that children who had just met an experimenter who broke a promise waited far less — so the wait partly measures whether a child expects the second treat to actually arrive, and the 2018 large replication by Watts, Duncan & Quan found the link to later outcomes much smaller and largely explained by family background.
title: The marshmallow test partly measures trust, not willpower

angle: Explains asymmetric dominance — shown by Huber, Payne and Puto in 1982 — where a third option that is clearly worse than one existing choice but not the other pulls preference toward the option that beats it, so the decoy is built to be rejected rather than bought, a shift standard rational-choice models say should not happen (Ariely's magazine-tier classroom demonstration being the well-known popular illustration, his own demo rather than a controlled replication).
title: The Decoy Effect: the option nobody picks still counts

angle: Bluma Zeigarnik's 1927 study found interrupted tasks were recalled more often than completed ones — but the modern productivity version oversells it, because later replications only find the effect when the person actually wanted to finish and the interruption felt like an interruption rather than a release.
title: Why unfinished tasks stick — but less reliably than told

angle: The Stanford prison experiment is remembered as ordinary men spontaneously turning brutal when handed power, but Zimbardo's own archives show guards were briefed to create an atmosphere of fear and corrected when judged too soft — and the careful replication, the BBC Prison Study by Reicher and Haslam, produced the opposite outcome, with guards failing to cohere and prisoners organising against them.
title: Stanford's Prison Guards Were Coached to Be Cruel

angle: The Kitty Genovese story that founded the bystander effect was largely bad journalism — a neighbour did go to her and someone did call police — yet the lab effect it inspired is real, while CCTV studies of actual street conflicts show that intervention happens in roughly nine out of ten cases and gets more likely as the crowd grows.
title: The 38 witnesses story was mostly wrong. The effect isn't.

angle: The 1999 study by Kruger and Dunning is real and reported that bottom-quarter scorers overestimated their rank while top scorers underrated theirs — but the famous rising-and-falling confidence curve was drawn later for the internet, and critics from Krueger and Mueller in 2002 to Gignac and Zajenkowski in 2020 argue the pattern is largely regression to the mean, a dispute Dunning still contests, leaving one durable takeaway: people misjudge their own competence in both directions.
title: The Dunning-Kruger chart isn't in the Dunning-Kruger paper

angle: The famous study is remembered as proof of blind obedience, but its own transcript points the other way: three prods that framed the shocks as reasonable science kept people going, while the fourth — "you have no other choice, you must go on" — produced more refusals than any other, suggesting people were being persuaded rather than commanded, and that plain authority is weaker than authority dressed as a worthwhile cause.
title: Milgram's fourth prod: the order people refused most

angle: The bell is the single most memorable element of the most famous experiment in psychology and it was largely a product of popularisation and translation — Pavlov's lab relied on metronomes, buzzers, whistles, tones, a harmonium, flashing lights and touch, because a bell's pitch and volume can't be held steady between trials and steady control was the entire point; the deeper distortion is that 'Pavlovian' now means mindless reflex, when the work was careful physiology of digestion by a man whose 1904 Nobel Prize was for digestion, not conditioning.
title: Pavlov's Bell: The Detail The Retelling Invented

angle: Phineas Gage's "no longer Gage" description is a snapshot from soon after his 1848 accident, while the best-documented part of his later life is years spent driving stagecoaches in Chile — a job demanding timekeeping, money handling and control of horse teams — which means the case is far better evidence for recovery than for permanent ruin.
title: Phineas Gage: the recovery half nobody teaches

angle: Rosenhan's 1973 paper is credited with forcing the overhaul of psychiatric diagnosis, yet Susannah Cahalan found his own admission record describes distressing voices, copper foil pressed over his ears and signs of danger to himself — a presentation that makes his admission a reasonable clinical call rather than the diagnostic failure the paper reported, which is a problem for the evidence even though the reform it triggered was probably needed anyway.
title: The copper over his ears: the study that rewrote psychiatry

angle: The default is genuinely one of the strongest levers in behavioural science — it doubled consent even in a randomised online experiment — but the consent gap is not the donation gap: presumed-consent countries run only roughly a quarter to a third higher in actual donations, and Spain, the country everyone cites as proof, sat unremarkable for a decade after its 1979 law and only moved once it built full-time hospital donor coordinators, which means the paperwork changed the answer while the staffing changed the outcome.
title: Austria: 99.98% consent. Germany: 12%. Same question.

angle: The famous 75 per cent is the share of participants who caved at least once across the whole run, not the share of answers — counted by response, roughly two thirds of answers on critical trials were independent, about a quarter of people never conformed at all, and when Asch gave the participant one confederate telling the truth, conformity collapsed to a fraction of its level, which is why he wrote that what struck him was people's independence.
title: Asch's line experiment: the 75% doesn't mean what you think

angle: Learned helplessness was taught for fifty years as the story of animals learning their actions were futile, until Maier and Seligman argued in 2016 that passivity is the brain's default under prolonged aversive events and control is the thing that must be learned — which flips therapy from arguing someone out of a belief to giving them repeated experiences of agency.
title: Learned Helplessness: Its Authors' Own 2016 Correction

angle: The 1998 ego depletion study found the radish group gave up sooner and launched the idea that willpower is a finite fuel tank — but when 23 labs ran one pre-agreed protocol on over 2,000 people in 2016, the pooled effect came out near zero, and a second large pre-registered test in 2021 found it very small or absent; the likeliest reason the original literature looked so solid is that studies finding the effect got published and those that didn't mostly didn't, and the glucose spin-off — that a sweet drink restores self-control — has fared worse still, though Baumeister disputes the replication's choice of task and that argument is still live.
title: 23 labs retested willpower. The effect came out near zero

angle: The 2010 power-posing study (42 participants) reported hormonal and risk-taking effects; a ~200-person replication in 2015 found the feeling of power held but the hormones and risk-taking did not, a 2017 p-curve analysis found no evidential value for those effects, and in 2016 the paper's own first author, Dana Carney, publicly wrote that she no longer believes them — while the milder claim, that posture changes how you feel, is still standing.
title: Power posing: the author who stopped believing her own study

angle: In Loftus and Palmer's 1974 study there was no broken glass in the film at all — the people who "remembered" it were the ones who had been asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed", which shows memory is assembled at the moment of recall from fragments and whatever the question implies, not replayed from a recording.
title: The broken glass that wasn't there: how memory rebuilds

angle: Robbers Cave was the second attempt at the study — the 1953 Middle Grove camp failed because the boys already knew each other, worked out the adults were staging the sabotage, and turned on the researchers instead, so the famous design quietly made sure the two groups met as strangers.
title: Robbers Cave failed once: the boys spotted the setup

angle: The replication rate is the headline everyone fights over, but the more unsettling number is what happened to the findings that did survive — at the median their effect size dropped from 0.25 to 0.10, roughly an 82 per cent cut in shared variance, meaning the real story is not fake effects but real effects that are a fraction of the size they were sold as.
title: 274 Social Science Claims Retested: Survivors Shrank

angle: They were right — there was no trick, and the horse still could not count; Hans was reading the involuntary tension in the questioner's body and stopping the instant it released, which is why the real failure was in the question the panel asked, not in their honesty, and why double-blind procedure exists at all.
title: 13 experts found no trick. The horse still couldn't count
